You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC

1. Parse the grid, caps, counters, and one-action JSON protocol. Treat every instance as independent. On every turn—including demo requests—emit exactly one permitted action JSON object and no commentary or tools; recheck counters before acting.
2. Infer a candidate transformation by identifying what differs between each input and output; explicitly note unchanged demos as evidence that the rule is conditional, identity-preserving, or only triggered by a feature absent there—not as proof of a particular rule. Compare dimensions, separators, color roles, object masks, counts, orientation, and exact edits; preserve untouched cells unless evidence says otherwise. For compressed/resized outputs, test partitioning and aggregation; for repeated grids, establish tile periods and separators; for panel copying, verify relative coordinates; for motif stamping, derive the source-to-marker offset. Do not generalize a coincidental overlap into a rule.
3. Spend demo requests when candidate rules remain underdetermined, especially before the first guess or after a wrong submission. Choose a demo that distinguishes plausible rules, and compare its exact changed cells against the input to infer the actual operation. When a recognized task id has a stored task-specific rule, treat it only as a hypothesis: verify that its grid dimensions, color roles, and demonstration signature match this instance before applying it. A wrong submission refutes the submitted output, not necessarily every part of the underlying rule; compare the proposed grid cell-by-cell with the rule-derived grid and the demonstrations before changing the rule. Avoid repeated speculative variants; request another discriminating demo when worthwhile.
4. Before submitting, build the complete grid from the supported rule and check every changed and unchanged region, dimensions, row count, row widths, and allowed colors. On every puzzle turn, the reply must contain only one permitted JSON action—no commentary, tools, or other text. Use `finish` only after the instance is over.

# Continual-ARC task-45977042 notes

Solved successfully (after 2 incorrect guesses and 2 demo requests). Family rule: the grid contains multiple hollow rectangular frames of different outline colors. Fill each enclosed zero-valued cavity, preserving the outlines and all outside cells. Fill color depends on the outline color: examples show outlines 3, 6, and 8 cavities filled with 2; outline 4 frame's single interior pixel becomes 7. In test, frames 1/5/8/9: interior cavities of 1 and 5 were color 2; 8 and 9 cavities were color 7. This is a mapping determined by outline/frame color, not cavity size. Demo 1: 3-outline 2x2 interior => 2; 6-outline 2x2 interior => 2; 1-outline 1x1 interior => 7. Demo 2 confirms 8-outline 4x4 interior => 2; 3-outline 1x2 interior => 2; 4-outline 1x1 interior => 7; 3-outline tall interior => 7. More precisely, apparent rule might be selected outline colors with output based on outline's shape/motif role, not simply color: in demo 2, 3 has multiple shapes and one cavity 1x5 filled 7 while other 3 cavities 2x2 filled 2. Test correct output: color 1 2x2 hole -> 2; color 5 2x2 hole ->2; color8 3x3 interior ->7; color9 3x3 interior ->7. So infer mapping using whole repeated patterns, not color alone.

Demos: Demo1 11x10: color3 hollow frame with 2x2 hole -> fill 2; color6 frame with 2x2 hole -> fill 2; color1 3x3 ring with singleton hole -> 7. Demo2 10x30: color8 frame with 4x4 interior -> 2; color3 frames: one 2x2 hole ->2; one 1x5 hole ->7; one 1x2 hole ->2; color4 frame singleton hole ->7. Successful test output was 11x21: interior row1-2 cols9-10 color2; color5 row6-7 cols1-2 color2; color8 rows6-8 cols6-8 color7; color9 rows5-7 cols15-17 color7 (0-based).

Caution: initial guesses used color-based mapping and got wrong; the actual distinguishing feature appears to be cavity dimensions: cavities matching a 2x2 square or 4x4 square filled 2? but test 3x3 squares for 8/9 were 7; demo2 4x4->2, 2x2->2, singleton->7, 1x5->7, 1x2->2. Could be exact structural rule not fully understood. Preserve frame borders and all non-hole pixels. In future recurring instances request demonstrations if uncertain; do not overgeneralize color map. Strictly validate grid widths.
